This book about artificial intelligence (AI) is long, and it is meant to be used, not only read. This section shows you how it is organized, so that you can find anything in any chapter and spend your time where it counts.

## Three Reading Paths {.unnumbered}

Every section of every chapter carries one of three tags, printed under its heading.

| Tag | What it means | Who reads it |
|---|---|---|
| **Core** | The main reading of each chapter. If your course has exams, only Core sections are examinable. | Everyone |
| **Studio** | Hands-on material for a lab session or for work at home on the chapter's assignment | Anyone in a course that uses the book; anyone who wants practice |
| **Deep** | An optional extension: more evidence, a technical detail, a little mathematics or Python. Not examinable. | Readers who want more |

Five whole chapters are Deep: Chapter 6 (Context Engineering and Reusable Workflows), Chapter 13 (Multimodal AI), Chapter 17 (Explainability and Transparency), Chapter 22 (The State of the Art) and Chapter 23 (Philosophical Debates). They are not examinable, but they are among the most useful chapters if your work leads that way. When a Core chapter needs a term from a Deep chapter, it defines that term again in its own Core text, so you never have to read a Deep chapter to follow the Core path.

## The Parts of Every Chapter {.unnumbered}

Every chapter follows the same pattern in the same order. Learn it once, and you can find anything anywhere. Boxes are told apart by their label, border and icon, never by color alone.

| Part | What it is | What to do with it |
|---|---|---|
| Chapter Map | A one-page visual map of the chapter, with the AI Work Loop and this chapter's step highlighted, and a short "at a glance" summary | Read first; return to it before the exam |
| Time | How long the Core reading and the whole Core package take | Plan your study time |
| Opening Case | A real, cited event that frames the chapter's problem; the chapter returns to it at the end | Keep its question in mind as you read |
| Learning Objectives | Four to six things you will be able to do, each tagged with one of the book's learning outcomes (LO1–LO7) and a framework | Use them as a checklist |
| Warm-up | Three ungraded questions answered from what you know today | Answer before reading; compare later |
| Core sections | Five to eight short sections, one idea each, each with at least one figure | The examinable reading |
| Check Yourself | Two or three recall questions at the end of each Core section | Answer without looking back, then check Appendix E |
| Worked Example → Faded Example → Your Turn | For each skill: a fully solved example, then a partly solved one with steps left for you, then free practice | Study the first, finish the second, do the third |
| Studio sections | The chapter's lab work and assignment steps | Do in a lab session or at home |
| Deep sections | Optional extensions, marked "Deep" | Read if you want more; not examinable |
| Hands-on Labs | Two to four tool-neutral lab tasks; current tool steps live in Compass | Do in a lab session or on your own |
| Case Study | A cited real-world case, labeled on the book's diagrams | Read it, then answer the Case Study Questions |
| Ethics Lens | The responsibility side of the chapter's topic | Discuss it |
| Career Connection | How the topic shows up in at least three occupations | Find your own field |
| From the Field | A short account drawn from the author's own published work | Connect the idea to practice |
| Chapter Summary and Key Terms | A visual summary card and the chapter's terms, all defined in the Glossary (Appendix A) | Review before exams |
| Review Questions A, B and C | A: terms and concepts; B: short cases with a justified decision; C: take a position and defend it. They mirror the three exam sections. | Exam practice |
| Spaced Review | Three to five questions on the chapters read just before this one | Keep earlier ideas fresh |
| Discussion Questions | Open questions, including one on ethics, one on careers and one across fields | For class and study groups |
| Application Assignment | The chapter's portfolio artifact, with a rubric and an alternative assignment | Submit as your instructor directs, or keep it; it feeds your portfolio |
| AI Use Declaration | A short statement attached to every assignment: tools used, purpose, what you accepted, rejected or revised, how you verified it, and where your judgment shaped the work | Write it for every artifact |
| Case Study Questions | Analysis questions on the chapter's case | Practice for exam section B |
| Mini-Project (optional) | A longer project that can feed your portfolio | Choose one if it fits your goals |
| Midterm Bridge and Final Bridge | A review figure and eight exam-format items at the end of Chapter 10 (midterm) and Chapter 21 (final), each pointing to the section to reread | Use before a midterm or final exam, or as a review of each half of the book |
| Further Reading and Compass Links | Selected readings with full references, and links to optional practice | Follow what interests you |

## Reading Order Is Not Always Chapter Order {.unnumbered}

The chapters are numbered in the order that makes sense for a book. A course can read the first eight in a slightly different order, so that each lab has what it needs: Chapters 5, 6 and 7 are written so that they do not depend on Chapter 4, which can come just before Chapter 8.

## One Possible Plan: Fifteen Weeks {.unnumbered}

The table below is **one suggested plan** for a fifteen-week semester with a concept session and a lab session each week. It is not the only way to use the book, and it carries no dates: your instructor, or you, decide the calendar.

| Week | Read | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Chapter 1 | Before the first lab session |
| 2 | Chapter 2, then Chapter 3 | Chapter 2 before the concept session; Chapter 3 before the lab session |
| 3 | Chapter 5 | Chapter 6 is the optional Deep extension |
| 4 | Chapter 7 | |
| 5 | Chapter 4, then Chapter 8 | Chapter 4 before the concept session; Chapter 8 before the lab session |
| 6–7 | Chapters 9 and 10 | |
| 8 | Review | A midterm, if the course has one (Chapter 10's Midterm Bridge) |
| 9–11 | Chapters 11, 12 and 14 | Chapter 13 is the optional Deep extension |
| 12 | Chapters 15, 16 and 18 | Chapter 17 is the optional Deep extension |
| 13 | Chapter 19 | |
| 14–15 | Chapter 20; Chapter 21 in two parts | Part A before a portfolio workshop, Part B before the portfolio is due |

Chapters 22 and 23 are Deep chapters for any point after Part I.

**Adapting the plan.** For a ten-week quarter, keep the order and pair weeks: Chapters 1–3 in weeks 1 and 2, Chapters 5, 7, 4 and 8 in weeks 3 and 4, Chapters 9–11 in weeks 5 and 6, Chapters 12 and 14 in week 7, Chapters 15, 16 and 18 in week 8, and Chapters 19–21 in weeks 9 and 10, leaving the Deep chapters to individual interest. For a shorter course, a workshop series or a professional-development module, choose a route below and assign the Core sections of those chapters only; each chapter defines its own terms, so none depends on reading every earlier one. If your instructor's schedule and this table differ, follow your instructor.

## How Long It Takes {.unnumbered}

Each chapter opens with a time statement. It gives two honest numbers, counted at 150 words a minute: the time for the Core sections, and the time for the whole Core package (the Core sections plus the case, the summary and the exercises you are expected to do). Each statement ends with the same reminder: allow more if you read more slowly or are reading in a second language.

Some chapters take longer than others, and each time statement says so rather than hiding it. Use the two numbers to plan, whatever pace your course or your own schedule sets.

## Where the Answers Are {.unnumbered}

Appendix E holds model answers to every Check Yourself question, every faded example and the odd-numbered end-of-chapter questions. Use them after you try, not before. Answers to even-numbered questions are in the instructor package, so instructors can use them for graded practice. Compass, the optional companion, also gives feedback on many questions ("Meet Compass").

## Companion Files {.unnumbered}

The labs and alternative assignments use provided materials: dated sample AI outputs, constructed data files, templates, and printable or screen-reader-friendly lab sheets. These are the book's companion files. They come with the book and are released with it under the same license, and the copyright page gives their address. When a chapter or lab says "in the book's companion files," this is where to look. Instructors may also post the files on their course site. The companion files are separate from Compass.

## Routes Through the Book {.unnumbered}

**If you are a student in a course that uses this book.** Read the assigned Core sections before the concept session, answer the Check Yourself boxes, and do the Your Turn activities. The lab session uses the Studio sections and produces a draft of the chapter's artifact, which you submit on your course site with its AI Use Declaration. Use the Warm-up and Spaced Review to keep earlier chapters fresh, and the Bridges before each exam your course sets.

**If you teach.** The chapters fit the fifteen-week plan above, with a concept session and a lab session each week, but they also stand alone. Each chapter defines its own terms, so you can assign chapters out of order. Rubrics are printed in the book. "Mapping to Frameworks" links the chapters to four AI literacy frameworks. The book's license allows noncommercial adaptation with credit, under the same license. Instructors who adopt the book can request the instructor package (lecture slides with speaker notes, the test bank and the even-numbered answers) by writing to the author at ses@sadievrenseker.com from an institutional address.

**If you are learning on your own.** Follow the Core path in chapter order. Do the worked, faded and Your Turn examples; they are the heart of the method. The labs work with free tools. Compass can track your progress and leads to an optional certificate.

**If you are a working professional.** Start with Chapter 1 and its AI Work Loop. Then pick by need: Chapters 4 and 8 (failure and verification), 5 and 12 (prompting and choosing tools), 14 (agents and oversight), 15 and 18 (privacy, law and governance), 19 (your field) and 21 (a personal code of practice). The Career Connection and From the Field boxes are written with you in mind.

## Exams and the Portfolio {.unnumbered}

If your course has exams, a natural split is a midterm on the Core sections of Chapters 1–10 and a final on the Core sections of the whole book, weighted to the second half. The book's exam practice uses three parts: terms and concepts, a case, and an interpretive question. Review Questions A, B and C practice exactly those parts. Appendix D adds a full-length practice exam.

The portfolio grows chapter by chapter. Each chapter's Application Assignment produces one artifact. At the end, you revise your strongest work, add a reflection and a personal AI code of practice (Chapter 21) and, if your instructor uses one, present it in a short oral defense. Chapter 20 shows how to present it to an employer or a graduate program.

## The Students in This Book {.unnumbered}

Five fictional students appear throughout the chapters: Lucia (accounting), Marcus (nursing), Maya (psychology), Sam (mechanical engineering) and Hana (media arts and design). They are invented composites, used to show the same skills in different fields, and they are never used as evidence. "Meet the Students" introduces them.

## Two Scales Used Throughout {.unnumbered}

When the book tells a real case, it says how firmly each fact is established. Three attribution tiers are used:

| Tier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Confirmed | Stated in the primary record |
| Reported | Stated by a named outlet or person |
| Inferred | The book's reading of the evidence |

When you check a claim, from Chapter 8 on, you give it one of five verdicts (wording from the Glossary):

| Verdict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Supported | The evidence says what the claim says |
| Partly supported | Part holds, part does not or is missing |
| Unsupported | No evidence for it at the stage you reached: nothing found, or the source does not say it |
| Contradicted | The evidence says otherwise |
| Cannot verify | The evidence exists or may exist, but you cannot reach it |

The book holds itself to nearly the same scale: its own fact-check gave every checked claim one of five verdicts, with "outdated" in the place of "contradicted" ("How This Book Was Written").
